subject: Biology
title: Alzheimer's Disease
description: A quick win: understand Alzheimer's Disease.

hook.text: Alzheimer's slowly erases memories, personality, and the ability to think. It affects 55 million people.

buildup.text: Abnormal proteins—amyloid plaques and tau tangles—build up in the brain and destroy neurons.

discovery.text: The disease starts decades before symptoms appear. Early damage hits the hippocampus first.

twist.text: Despite billions in research, there is still no cure. Only treatments that modestly slow decline.

climax.text: New drugs targeting amyloid show some promise, but prevention and early detection remain critical.

punchline.text: The cruelest disease steals who you are.

quiz.question: What proteins build up in the brain during Alzheimer's?

details.summary: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder where amyloid plaques and tau tangles accumulate in the brain, destroying neurons and synapses. It begins with mild memory loss and gradually erases personality, language, and the ability to function.
details.whyItMatters: Alzheimer's affects over 50 million people worldwide with no cure. Understanding its biology is critical for developing treatments and supporting the millions of caregivers navigating this devastating disease.
takeaways: Amyloid plaques and tau tangles destroy neurons progressively
Early symptoms involve short-term memory loss before spreading
Current treatments slow symptoms but cannot reverse damage

faq.question: What causes Alzheimer's disease?
faq.answer: The exact cause remains debated. Amyloid-beta protein fragments accumulate into plaques between neurons, and tau protein forms tangles inside neurons. Both disrupt cell communication and trigger inflammation, but whether they are causes or consequences is still studied.

faq.question: Can Alzheimer's disease be prevented?
faq.answer: No guaranteed prevention exists, but regular exercise, social engagement, cognitive stimulation, cardiovascular health, and quality sleep are associated with reduced risk. Genetics play a role, but lifestyle factors significantly influence onset timing.
